question: A skeletal survey of an unidentified individual yields a complete femur, a partial tibia (mid-shaft fragment only), and no other long bones. Which statement best describes the approach to stature estimation?

answers.text: Use the femur length alone in a regression formula; the tibia fragment is unusable.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Stature estimation relies on the complete length of long bones (femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, radius, ulna) using regression equations (e.g., Trotter & Gleser, India-specific Pearson's formula). A mid-shaft tibia fragment cannot yield a reliable total bone length, so the femur alone is used.

answers.text: Average the stature estimates from both the femur and the tibia fragment.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Averaging requires valid length measurements from each bone. A mid-shaft fragment does not give a reliable total bone length, so it cannot contribute a stature estimate to be averaged.

answers.text: Use skull dimensions as a substitute because all long bones are incomplete or unavailable.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The skull is not used for stature estimation. Stature is derived from long bone lengths using established regression formulae. The femur is complete here and should be used.

answers.text: Defer stature estimation entirely; partial remains are inadmissible for medicolegal reporting.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Even a single complete long bone provides a valid stature estimate with a stated confidence interval. A medicolegal opinion should be given using available evidence, with appropriate qualification of limitations.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: stature estimation requires complete bone length measurements. Use only the bones for which total length can be reliably determined; here, only the complete femur qualifies.
Well done. In forensic practice, use all complete long bones available; report a range with confidence intervals and clearly state which bones were and were not used.
